\title{Which Parts of BM25 Help Learned Top-$k$ Selection?\\
Tests in Sparse Retrieval, KV-Cache Page Selection and Expert Routing}

\begin{abstract}
Learned sparse retrieval, KV-cache page selection and mixture-of-experts routing all keep
the top $k$ items by a learned score. Lexical retrieval corrects that score with BM25's
inverse document frequency (IDF), saturation and length normalisation, and the other two
usually do not. We score fourteen weak sparse codes of one frozen encoder under all eight
on/off combinations of the three components on thirteen collections. The correction raises
nDCG@10 in 162 of the 179 main-grid rows where the margin is defined. A predictor
registered in advance from the frequency curve does no better than always predicting a
gain. Exact Shapley values assign $62\%$ of the gain to saturation, which reads only the
document. Tests fixed in advance confirm that saturation's effect follows the
dispersion of the stored values. Whether IDF and length normalisation help varies with
representation and corpus, and a label-free rule based on agreement with text BM25 gets
its sign right on new MS~MARCO rows and on SPLADE-v3 no more often than a constant. In KV
selection and routing we take an item's frequency to be how often the selector chose it
during calibration. With IDF on, the pages chosen hold $0.29$ to $0.44$ of the attention
mass, against $0.90$ to $0.95$ without, mean RULER accuracy falls from $0.71$ and $0.78$
to at most $0.046$, and mean MMLU accuracy on OLMoE falls from $0.480$ to between $0.382$ and $0.390$. The
retrieval predictor, applied without refitting, predicts a gain everywhere and is wrong in
sign on 24 of 24 KV rows and 52 of 55 MMLU subjects.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

A learned sparse retriever scores a query against a document by an inner product over
non-negative features and returns the top $k$ \citep{formal2021splade,nguyen2023unified}.
Quest scores the pages of a key-value cache against the current query and attends only to
the best ones \citep{tang2024quest}. A mixture-of-experts router scores every expert and
sends the token to the top $k$ \citep{shazeer2017moe,fedus2022switch}. All three keep the
top $k$ items by a score that is or can be made non-negative, so the BM25 correction of
Section~\ref{sec:problem} can be applied to each (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}). In retrieval the score is a sum over many features. For a KV
page or an expert it is a single number, which limits what saturation can do
(Section~\ref{sec:transfer}).

Lexical retrieval corrects the raw score. BM25 discounts features that occur throughout the
collection, stops rewarding repeated evidence past a point and adjusts for document length
\citep{sparckjones1972idf,robertson2009bm25}. Each part was designed for words, and applied
to learned features BM25 has both helped and hurt. On one benchmark suite BM25 beats the
inner product by $0.20$ nDCG@10 on sparse-autoencoder features and loses by $0.11$ on
SPLADE-v3 \citep{clavie2026latent}. The explanation offered is that BM25 helps while a
vocabulary keeps a Zipfian frequency curve \citep{clavie2026latent,han2026bm25v}. If that
is right, statistics of the frequency curve should predict the sign of the gain before the
experiment is run.

We tested this prediction in retrieval and in two other top-$k$ selections, and it failed
in all three. Fourteen sparse codes of one frozen encoder were
scored under all eight combinations of the three components on thirteen collections. The
correction helped almost everywhere, and the registered predictor did not predict where it
helped more. Most of the gain comes from saturation, a component that uses no collection
statistics. The dispersion of the stored values predicts the size of saturation's effect, a
relation confirmed on held-out parameter settings. Index statistics predicted little of
whether IDF and length normalisation help. A relevance proxy predicts part of it, and
on SPLADE-v3 the registered version fails. In KV selection and routing we take an item's
frequency to be how often the selector chose it during calibration. IDF then moves the
budget to items the selector rarely chooses, and accuracy falls in both.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item A controlled grid of fourteen representations from one encoder under all eight
configurations on thirteen collections, $1{,}358$ rows, with an exact Shapley
decomposition of the gain (Section~\ref{sec:attribution}).
\item Six tests registered in advance (Table~\ref{tab:registered}). One, a set of six
hypotheses on saturation, passes. One has no pass mark in retrieval and predicts almost
nothing. The other four fail their pass marks. Among them is the label-free rule in KV
selection, which chooses correctly on every row but cannot meet its sign mark because every
row has the same sign. We give a likely reason for each failure (Sections~\ref{sec:retrieval},
\ref{sec:splade} and~\ref{sec:transfer}).
\item A mechanism for saturation, confirmed by tests fixed in advance, and evidence that
index statistics predict the value of saturation but not that of collection statistics,
and a label-free rule for the latter tested with three references on new rows and on
SPLADE-v3 (Sections~\ref{sec:predicts} to~\ref{sec:splade}).
\item Measurements of the correction in KV selection and routing, a label-free check with
exact attention mass, and a proof that without IDF saturation cannot change a selection
with one score per item (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Term weighting and learned sparse retrieval.} IDF began as a statistical account
of term specificity \citep{sparckjones1972idf}. Saturation approximates the two-Poisson
model of within-document frequency \citep{robertson1994poisson}, and length normalisation
was pivoted so that long documents are neither favoured nor penalised
\citep{singhal1996pivoted}. BM25 combines the three \citep{robertson2009bm25}. Learned
sparse retrievers learn term weights and score by inner product, through contextual exact
match \citep{gao2021coil} or expansion over the subword vocabulary in SPLADE
\citep{formal2021splade,formal2021spladev2,lassance2024spladev3}.

\paragraph{BM25 on learned features.} Sparse autoencoders decompose dense activations into
many non-negative features \citep{cunningham2024sae,gao2025topksae}. \citet{clavie2026latent}
score SAE features of a frozen dense retriever with BM25 and report $0.582$ nDCG@10 against
$0.381$ for the inner product, and the reverse on SPLADE-v3, $0.455$ against $0.568$. CL-SR
loses 11 to 18 percent of its nDCG@10 on TREC-DL without IDF \citep{park2025clsr}.
\citet{han2026bm25v} find BM25 and the inner product about equal on image features and credit
top-$k$ filtering for suppressing what IDF would down-weight. SPLARE and SAE-SPLADE build
SAE-based sparse retrievers that score by inner product \citep{formal2026splare,zong2026tokens}.
None of these varies the representation systematically or separates all three components.

\paragraph{Predicting effectiveness without labels.} Query performance prediction estimates
retrieval quality from the query and the ranking
\citep{carmel2010difficulty,cronen2002clarity,shtok2012nqc}. Systems can be ranked without judgements
against pseudo-relevant documents from pooled output \citep{soboroff2001ranking}. Our
label-free predictor applies this pseudo-relevance idea to a new target, the difference
between two scorers.

\paragraph{Selection inside the transformer.} Quest scores KV pages against page min-max key
summaries \citep{tang2024quest}. H2O keeps recent tokens and heavy hitters, the tokens that
have received the most attention \citep{zhang2023h2o}. SnapKV keeps the positions an
observation window attends to \citep{li2024snapkv}, StreamingLLM keeps the first keys as
attention sinks \citep{xiao2024streamingllm} and Expected Attention prunes KV pairs that future
queries are predicted to attend to little \citep{devoto2025expectedattention}. Mixture-of-experts layers
route each token to its top-$k$ experts \citep{shazeer2017moe,lepikhin2021gshard,fedus2022switch},
balanced by an auxiliary loss \citep{zoph2022stmoe} or a load-driven bias
\citep{wang2024lossfree}. We know of no work that applies BM25's components to KV
selection or routing.

\section{Problem and Registered Tests}
\label{sec:problem}

\paragraph{The correction.} For query and document vectors $x_q, x_d$ with non-negative
coordinates we score
\begin{equation}
S(q,d) = \sum_{j} x_{qj}\, w_j\, T(x_{dj}, \ell_d).
\label{eq:scorer}
\end{equation}
The weight $w_j$ is one or $\idf_j = \ln(1 + (N - df_j + 0.5)/(df_j + 0.5))$, where $df_j$
of the $N$ documents have feature $j$. The length factor $\ell_d$ is one or
$1 - b + b L_d/\overline{L}$ with $L_d = \sum_j x_{dj}$. The transform $T(f,\ell)$ is
$f/\ell$ or the saturated $(k_1+1)f/(f + k_1\ell)$. Length normalisation without
saturation divides each value by $\ell_d$, a variant BM25 does not contain. A configuration is a bit string in the
order IDF, saturation, length. Configuration \texttt{000} is the plain inner product and
\texttt{111} is BM25. IDF and length normalisation read collection statistics; saturation
reads only the document.

\paragraph{Rows and targets.} One row pairs a representation with a collection at a support
budget, BM25 parameters $(k_1, b)$ and a basis seed, and carries eight nDCG@10 values $Q_c$.
The registered target is the margin $m = (Q_{111} - Q_{000})/\operatorname{sd}(Q_{000},
\ldots, Q_{111})$. The Shapley value of switch $s$ averages its marginal effect over every
order in which the switches can be turned on \citep{shapley1953value}. Writing $Q_A$ for the
configuration with the switches in $A$ on,
\begin{equation}
\phi_s = \sum_{A \not\ni s}
\tfrac{|A|!\,(2-|A|)!}{6}\bigl(Q_{A\cup\{s\}} - Q_{A}\bigr),
\label{eq:shapley}
\end{equation}
and the three values sum to $Q_{111} - Q_{000}$. The collection gain $G = Q_{111} - Q_{010}$
is the value of IDF and length normalisation once saturation is applied, and its sign
answers the practical question of whether to use collection statistics.

\paragraph{Predictors.} The pre-registered predictor is a ridge regression of $m$ on three
diagnostics of the frequency curve. The label-free predictor replaces $Q_c$ by a
pseudo-quality $\tilde{Q}_c$, the agreement of configuration $c$ with a reference that
needs no labels. The substitution gives estimates $\tilde{\phi}_s$ and $\tilde{G}$ with no
fitted parameter. Its decision rule uses collection statistics where $\tilde{G} > 0$. A
second, fitted predictor regresses each target on the pre-registered diagnostics, index
statistics, ranking features (the spread of each configuration's top-100 scores, the
relative gap between its first and tenth scores, and the top-10 overlap between
configurations that differ in one switch) and the pseudo-qualities.

\paragraph{Transfer.} Eq.~\eqref{eq:scorer} applies to any selection with a non-negative
score and a frequency count. For KV page $i$ in each head the value is the softplus of
Quest's criticality, its upper bound on the query-key product from the page's key minima
and maxima, divided by the median selected value of the head during calibration. Its
frequency $\sfreq_i$ is the fraction of the calibration positions at or after the page at
which Quest selects it, and its IDF uses that number of positions in place of $N$. Its
length is the norm of its concatenated key minima and maxima.
For expert $e$ the value is the router probability, the frequency is the share of
calibration tokens routed to $e$ and the length, shared by all experts for a token, is the
norm of that token's router logits. Because that length is shared, length normalisation
cannot change which experts are selected unless IDF and saturation are both on, and by
Proposition~\ref{prop:single} saturation cannot change them without IDF. Configurations \texttt{000} to
\texttt{011} therefore route identically up to ties, as do \texttt{100} and \texttt{101}. The selected experts keep their original gate
weights. A row is a task and token budget in
attention and a benchmark or MMLU subject in routing. The predictor fitted in retrieval is
applied without refitting.

\paragraph{Registration.} The tests in Table~\ref{tab:registered} come from the project
proposal (August), a hypotheses file (29 September) and a registration file (20 October).
Each was committed to the repository before the predictions it tests were computed, and,
except for SPLADE-v3, before the outcomes existed or were read. The
limit of $1.81$ on mean absolute error (MAE) is $1.5$ times the corpus-held-out RMSE in
retrieval ($1.21$). The interim report (2 October) added the condition of beating the
majority sign, before any transfer run, because always predicting a gain is
already right on $90\%$ of the 179 retrieval rows. A predictor that does not beat the constant prediction of the retrieval
majority sign has not shown transfer. The better of the two constant signs on the transfer
rows is reported as the strictest comparison, and the label-free rule must exceed it.

\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Representations.} All representations come from \texttt{multilingual-e5-base}
\citep{wang2024me5} at a pinned revision. Seven bases are fitted on the same $200{,}000$
MS~MARCO passages \citep{bajaj2016msmarco}: split-rectified identity, Gaussian projection
(768), PCA (384), soft $k$-means over $4{,}096$ centroids, product and residual quantisation
($8 \times 256$, \citealp{jegou2011pq,chen2010rq}) and a Top-$K$ SAE with $8{,}192$ features
of which at most 32 are active. Pooled granularity applies each basis to the mean of the
token states and token granularity to each state before summing. The two granularities
give fourteen representations. Supports are capped at 32 query and 128 document features in the primary
budget, and document frequency, lengths and IDF come from the capped vectors of each
corpus. Retrieval is exact over the whole corpus with $k_1 = 1.2$ and $b = 0.75$.

\paragraph{Collections and families.} The thirteen collections come from eleven corpora:
MS~MARCO dev with TREC-DL 2019 and 2020 on the same documents, six BEIR sets
\citep{thakur2021beir}, LIMIT \citep{weller2025limit} and the Hindi, Bengali and Telugu
portions of MIRACL \citep{zhang2023miracl}. Each sensitivity family varies one setting
(Table~\ref{tab:families} in the appendix). SPLADE-v3 \citep{lassance2024spladev3}, with its own backbone,
is scored under the same eight configurations as an external comparison.


\paragraph{Significance and diagnostics.} A paired bootstrap over queries with $10{,}000$
draws ($2{,}000$ for SPLADE-v3 and the transfer settings) recomputes numerator and denominator, with Holm correction \citep{holm1979} within each
pre-declared family. The pre-registered diagnostics are the Zipf slope of the
feature-frequency curve, IDF variance and the activation share of the most frequent $1\%$
of features. Index statistics describe the stored values, chiefly $\mathrm{cv}_x$, the
coefficient of variation of the stored document values. For the pseudo-quality
$\tilde{Q}_c$ in retrieval, the top 10 of a reference retriever on the same query is taken
as relevant and the stored top-100 list of configuration $c$ is scored by nDCG@10. The
references are text BM25, the dense encoder and the two fused by reciprocal rank.

\paragraph{KV-page selection.} The attention model is Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct
\citep{qwen2025qwen25} in float16. Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct was the planned model. Qwen,
fixed as the fallback before any run, was used because Llama was not accessible to us when the run started. All thirteen RULER tasks \citep{hsieh2024ruler} are run at a 4K context,
with 100 examples per task and token budgets of 512 and 1{,}024 over sixteen-token pages.
Prefill is dense and decoding attends only to the selected pages. Page frequencies come
from 64 causal positions of each example's own prompt. Full attention, Quest and H2O
\citep{zhang2023h2o} are run beside the eight configurations. Configuration \texttt{000}
runs Quest's scoring, and the two agree on every example. The label-free reference is exact attention mass,
the share of full-attention softmax mass that falls on the pages a configuration would
select, measured along the full-attention generation.

\paragraph{Expert routing.} OLMoE-1B-7B \citep{muennighoff2025olmoe} routes each token to 8
of 64 experts. The correction changes which experts run and keeps their gate weights.
Quality is the negative token log-likelihood on WikiText-2 \citep{merity2017wikitext} in
2{,}048-token windows and zero-shot accuracy on each of the 57 MMLU subjects
\citep{hendrycks2021mmlu}, scored by the likelihood of each choice. Frequencies come from
256 windows of 2{,}048 tokens from the WikiText-2 training split or from the subject's own prompts. A load-driven
frequency bias, the analogue of loss-free balancing \citep{wang2024lossfree}, is run beside
the eight configurations.

\section{Results in Retrieval}
\label{sec:retrieval}

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{5pt}
\input{tables/tab_quality}
\caption{nDCG@10 of text BM25 and the dense encoder, the mean over the fourteen sparse codes
under the inner product (\texttt{000}) and the full correction (\texttt{111}), the best code
under \texttt{111}, and SPLADE-v3 under both. MIRACL is outside SPLADE-v3's vocabulary.}
\label{tab:quality}
\end{table*}

\subsection{The correction helps the E5 codes}

Under the inner product the mean nDCG@10 of the capped sparse codes is at most $0.135$ on
every collection (Table~\ref{tab:quality}). The full correction raises their mean on every collection, and
the margin is positive in 162 of the 179 primary rows where it is defined ($90\%$). Holm-corrected,
all-on beats all-off in 134 of the 182 primary rows. After correction the best code, the
token-level SAE on twelve of the thirteen collections, beats text BM25 on six. Even so, full correction
is the strict best of the eight configurations in only 42 of the 182 primary rows, and the
mean of \texttt{011} ($0.163$) is above that of \texttt{111} ($0.158$), so adding IDF to
saturation and length normalisation lowers mean nDCG@10. The inner product scores below
$0.01$ in 81 of the 182 rows, so nearly any correction beats it.

\subsection{The registered predictor predicts almost nothing}

The primary ridge model explains almost none of the held-out variance of $m$, with $R^2$ of
$0.04$ across basis families and $0.02$ across corpora, and its sign accuracy equals that of
always predicting a gain. Part of the failure lies in the target. Of the margins, $85\%$
fall between $1.5$ and $3.5$, because in many rows $Q_{000}$ is near zero and every other
configuration is far above it. That leaves little variation for a diagnostic to explain.

\subsection{Where the gain comes from}
\label{sec:attribution}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{2.4pt}
\input{tables/tab_shapley}
\caption{Mean Shapley value of each switch (Eq.~\ref{eq:shapley}) and their sum
$Q_{111} - Q_{000}$, in each setting's metric: nDCG@10 in retrieval, accuracy in KV
selection and MMLU, and log-likelihood per token on WikiText.}
\label{tab:shapley}
\end{table}

Saturation carries most of the gain in each E5 family in Table~\ref{tab:shapley}.
Over the 182 primary rows it takes $62\%$, length normalisation $28\%$ and IDF $10\%$, so
collection statistics account for $38\%$ ($95\%$ interval $36$ to $41\%$, resampling
collections). IDF, the
component the Zipfian account is about, contributes least. As supports grow the share of IDF
shrinks and that of length grows, and at native support IDF's mean value is slightly
negative. \citet{han2026bm25v} report the same trend for image features, where document
frequencies converge as more features are active. On ArguAna, NFCorpus
and SciFact, shuffling the document frequencies turns IDF's mean Shapley value negative,
and the real value is larger in $83\%$ of the 42 rows (one-sided Wilcoxon $p < 10^{-6}$).
Uniform frequencies, which remove IDF, do not lower all-on nDCG@10 there ($0.157$ against
$0.147$ with the real frequencies, $p = 0.15$).

\subsection{What the index predicts}
\label{sec:predicts}

With length normalisation off, saturation maps a stored value $f$ to
$g(f) = (k_1+1)f/(f+k_1)$, and $g(f)/f$ falls as $f$ grows. If every stored value in the
index were equal, $g$ would rescale every score by one factor and the ranking would not
move. The more unequal the values, the more the ranking can move, so for a given $k_1$
and set of queries the dispersion of the stored values bounds how far saturation can move
a ranking. In our codes that move usually helps
($\phi_{\mathrm{sat}} > 0$ in $79\%$ of primary rows), so the index also predicts
$\phi_{\mathrm{sat}}$. Pooled PQ and RQ store equal values with equal lengths and their
saturation and length effects are exactly zero in every row (Table~\ref{tab:bases} in the
appendix). IDF and length normalisation also move the ranking by an amount the index fixes.
Whether those moves help depends on whether long documents were over-rewarded and whether
rare features separate relevant documents from the rest. For the strongest codes,
token-level SAE and token-level PCA, collection statistics help after saturation on fewer
than half the collections. In our rows index statistics predict little of whether those moves help (held-out
$R^2$ of $0.01$ to $0.12$ for $G$, Table~\ref{tab:predictor}). We take relevance to be the
missing input and test this in Section~\ref{sec:proxy}.


We committed six hypotheses before running them, on the $k_1$ and $b$ sweep of five
collections, rows the exploration had not used (Table~\ref{tab:confirm} in the appendix). All six pass. H5
holds by construction and checks the code, and H1 overlaps the primary rows. H2, H3, H4 and
H6 test the mechanism. A ridge model of $\phi_{\mathrm{sat}}$ on $\mathrm{cv}_x$ fitted at
$k_1 = 1.2$ ranks $\phi_{\mathrm{sat}}$ at $k_1 = 0.6$ and $2.4$ with Spearman $0.87$ and
$0.90$.

\subsection{Supplying relevance without labels}
\label{sec:proxy}

If what the index lacks is relevance, a proxy for relevance should restore the
prediction. Only the pseudo-label tier reaches positive held-out $R^2$ on every target
and axis (Table~\ref{tab:predictor} in the appendix). Within a row the pseudo-quality orders the eight
configurations like the true one, with a median Spearman correlation of $0.98$. On the
primary rows, which were available when the rule was designed, the unfitted rule raises
mean nDCG@10 from $0.159$ for always using collection statistics to $0.163$, against
$0.165$ for an oracle ($59\%$ of the headroom).

The interim report fixed this rule before the 84 MS~MARCO budget rows were produced. On those
rows $\tilde{G}$ ranks $G$ well (Spearman $0.91$ with the BM25 reference), but its sign is
right on $0.87$ of rows against $0.88$ for always predicting a gain. With the dense or fused
reference it is right on $0.95$, but the dense reference is the encoder the codes come
from (Section~\ref{sec:discussion}). The headroom is small, with always-on at $0.202$ and the
oracle at $0.203$. The three collections share one corpus, so these rows are not independent.

\section{The Correction on SPLADE-v3}
\label{sec:splade}

SPLADE-v3 under the inner product is far stronger than any of our codes, and the
correction lowers its nDCG@10 on 8 of 10 collections, from a mean of $0.523$ to $0.509$
(Table~\ref{tab:quality}). It is significantly worse on four collections and better on ArguAna and LIMIT
(bootstrap $p < 0.05$, uncorrected). The direction matches the reversal of \citet{clavie2026latent}; the size,
$0.014$ against their $0.113$, does not. Length normalisation accounts for the harm. Its
Shapley value is $-0.073$ (Table~\ref{tab:shapley}), but most of that comes from the
configurations that divide by length without saturation, which lower mean nDCG@10 by
$0.12$ to $0.13$. Inside BM25, turning length normalisation off raises it by $0.019$ ($0.528$ for
\texttt{110} against $0.509$). Saturation's Shapley value of $0.048$ comes from undoing that
division. On its own it changes mean nDCG@10 by less than $0.01$.

Here the sign of $G$ splits five to five, so a constant sign scores only $0.50$. With the
registered BM25 reference the label-free test fails. Its sign is right on half the
collections and its correlation with $G$ is $-0.04$. On the three MS~MARCO collections,
adding IDF and length normalisation raises agreement with BM25 by $0.06$ to $0.08$ while
lowering nDCG@10. Agreement with BM25 rewards a configuration for behaving like BM25, the
bias the registration named in advance. The secondary dense reference meets both marks,
with sign accuracy $0.70$ and a rule at $0.519$ against $0.509$ for always-on and $0.515$
for never using collection statistics, though over ten collections the interval for the
gain over always-on includes zero. The fused reference fails.

\section{Transfer to KV Pages and Experts}
\label{sec:transfer}

\subsection{KV-page selection}

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.5pt}
\input{tables/tab_attention}
\caption{Mean RULER accuracy over the 13 tasks at a 4K context, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct,
100 examples per task, and the mean share of full attention's softmax mass that falls on
the pages each configuration would select. Quest equals \texttt{000} on every example.
Configurations with IDF on are \texttt{100} to \texttt{111}.}
\label{tab:attention}
\end{table*}

With IDF on, page selection fails (Table~\ref{tab:attention}). Every configuration with IDF on falls to a mean accuracy of
$0.015$ to $0.046$, against $0.71$ and $0.78$ for Quest at the two budgets. The
configurations without IDF stay within $0.02$ of Quest. All-on is significantly worse than
all-off in all 24 rows with a defined margin after Holm correction, and better in none. $G$
is negative in all 24 rows. The
mean Shapley value of IDF is $-0.775$, against $-0.003$ for saturation and $0.002$ for length
(Table~\ref{tab:shapley}). Variable tracking scores zero under every mode, full attention
included (see the limitations), so its two rows have no defined margin.

A page's $\sfreq_i$, as we defined it, is Quest's own selection rate during calibration, so
IDF down-weights the pages Quest selected most often, and the outcome is partly fixed by
this definition. On the 100 examples of the first single-needle task at the larger budget, the
page holding the needle is selected in $0.82$ to $1.00$ of its calibration opportunities
and ranks between second and tenth of 210 to 247 pages. The first page is selected in
$0.96$ of its opportunities and the median page in about $0.5$. A page selected at all 64
calibration positions gets the smoothed IDF $\ln(1 + 0.5/64.5) \approx 0.008$ and one never
selected gets $\ln 130 \approx 4.9$, so the corrected score favours the pages Quest rarely
selects.

\begin{proposition}
\label{prop:single}
When each item carries a single score $f_i \ge 0$, as a KV page or an expert does, and IDF
is off, the saturated score is a strictly increasing function of $f_i/\ell_i$ and selects
the same top $k$ as the unsaturated score, up to ties.
\end{proposition}

It holds because $(k_1+1)f/(f+k_1\ell) = g(f/\ell)$ and $g$ is strictly increasing on
$f \ge 0$. With IDF on, $\idf_i\,g(f_i)$ and $\idf_i f_i$ can order pages differently,
and \texttt{110} and \texttt{100} give different answers on 92 of $2{,}600$ examples.
Without IDF, \texttt{010} and \texttt{000} differ on 38 and \texttt{011} and \texttt{001}
on 11, which we attribute to ties in float16 scores.

The registered predictor predicts a gain on all 24 rows and gets the sign wrong on all of
them, with a mean absolute error of $4.18$ against the limit of $1.81$. Its predictions
range only from $2.13$ to $2.21$, so it predicts a gain for nearly any input, and its
failure here says little about page frequency.

The registered label-free rule takes exact attention mass as its reference. Along each
full-attention generation, and averaged over tasks, the pages a configuration with IDF on
would select hold $0.29$ to $0.44$ of the softmax mass, against $0.90$ to $0.95$ without
IDF (Table~\ref{tab:attention}). On every task each configuration with IDF on holds less
mass than any without. $\tilde{G}$ is therefore negative on every
row. The rule's sign is right on all 24, against none for the retrieval majority sign, and
its mean accuracy over the 26 rows, $0.742$, equals the oracle's, against $0.024$ for
always-on. It still
fails the registered test, because when every row has the same sign the better constant
also scores $1.00$, a flaw in the pass mark we did not foresee. Across rows $\tilde{G}$ and
$G$ correlate at $-0.32$, so the rule gets the direction but not the size. Output agreement
with full attention, the secondary reference, gives the same decisions.

\subsection{Expert routing}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\input{tables/tab_routing}
\caption{OLMoE-1B-7B: mean zero-shot accuracy over the 57 MMLU subjects ($14{,}042$
questions) and WikiText-2 perplexity, for the native router, the load-driven frequency
bias and the eight configurations. Configurations in one row route identically.}
\label{tab:routing}
\end{table}

Configuration \texttt{000} calls the native forward pass. As
Proposition~\ref{prop:single} and the shared token length predict, \texttt{001} to
\texttt{011} give the same score as \texttt{000} on every example, and \texttt{101} the
same as \texttt{100} (Table~\ref{tab:routing}). With IDF on, mean MMLU accuracy falls
from $0.480$ to between $0.382$ and $0.390$ and WikiText perplexity rises from $7.49$ to
$7.86$ and $7.88$. All-on is worse than all-off on 52 subjects, better on 3 and tied on 2,
and after Holm correction it is significantly worse in 22 of the 58 rows and better in
none. As in KV selection, an expert's frequency is the router's own selection rate during
calibration, so IDF sends tokens towards experts the router rarely chooses. The frequency
bias, which adds a load-balancing term to the router probability instead of multiplying
it, costs less (MMLU $0.428$, perplexity $7.73$). The registered predictor gives $2.05$ to $2.18$
for every subject, and its sign is right on 3 of the 55 subjects with a nonzero margin
($0.05$), with an MAE of $3.98$ against the limit of $1.81$. On WikiText it predicts $2.19$
against a margin of $-2.07$. No label-free rule was registered for routing, because the
dense softmax mixture named in the interim report was not implemented.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

Saturation can change a selection only when an item's score is not a monotone function of
one value, as with a sum over features in retrieval or an IDF weight times the single score
of a page or expert (Proposition~\ref{prop:single}).

No index statistic predicts the value of collection statistics in our data. It varies across
representations and corpora and the frequency curve does not predict it. The rule built on
agreement with BM25 gains a little on the primary rows, gets the sign right no more often
than a constant on the new MS~MARCO rows and is right half the time on SPLADE-v3. Agreement
with BM25 rewards BM25-like scoring, so on SPLADE-v3, where BM25-like scoring hurts, it
favours the wrong configurations. The dense reference passes on SPLADE-v3 but may favour the E5 codes, which come from
its embedding.

The KV and routing results concern one definition of frequency, the selector's own
selection rate during calibration. Under it IDF down-weights the items the selector chose
most often during calibration. In KV selection the pages chosen instead hold less of the
exact attention mass, and accuracy falls in both settings. A frequency that does not come from the selector, such as one counted over
unrelated prompts, was not tested.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

BM25's correction raises the quality of weak sparse codes of a frozen encoder in nine rows
out of ten, mostly through saturation, and lowers the quality of SPLADE-v3, mostly through
length normalisation. The registered frequency-curve predictor predicts almost nothing in
retrieval, and in KV-page selection its near-constant prediction of a gain is wrong on every
row and in routing on 52 of 55 subjects. Stored-value dispersion predicts
saturation's Shapley value in tests fixed in advance. A rule built on agreement with BM25
chooses collection statistics slightly better than always using them on the primary rows,
but on new MS~MARCO rows its sign is no more accurate than a constant and on SPLADE-v3 it
is right half the time. With frequency taken as the selector's own selection rate, IDF
selects KV pages holding on average $0.29$ to $0.44$ of the attention mass and accuracy
falls to at most $0.046$. Exact attention mass, used without labels, picks the right
setting on every row, but so does the constant choice, and the registered test fails. In
routing IDF lowers mean MMLU accuracy from $0.480$ to between $0.382$ and $0.390$.

\section*{Challenges, Limitations and Future Work}
\label{sec:limitations}

One encoder underlies every retrieval code, so basis and encoder effects cannot be
separated, and E5 saw MIRACL in training. The SPLADE comparison covers one model on ten
collections. The KV-page runs use one 4K context and 100 examples per task instead of 500,
a cut for compute stated before any outcome was read. Variable tracking was not measured,
because the prompts lack RULER's answer prefix. The label-free sign mark cannot be met
when every row has the same sign, as in KV selection. Routing is tested at inference on
one model, with MMLU frequencies from each subject's own prompts. A frequency counted over
unrelated prompts is the next test.
